content: Endometriosis is a prevalent gynecological condition characterized by the presence of endometrial-like tissue outside the uterine cavity, excluding adenomyosis. This condition often manifests with significant pain. Gonadotrophin-releasing hormone analogues (GnRHas) are one therapeutic option offered to premenopausal women to alleviate this pain. These medications can be administered via intranasal delivery, subcutaneous injection, or intramuscular injection. The mechanism of action of GnRHas involves the downregulation of the pituitary gland, leading to a hypogonadotropic hypogonadal state. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of GnRHas in managing the painful symptoms associated with endometriosis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in April 2010 across multiple electronic databases, including the Cochrane Menstrual Disorders and Subfertility Group specialist register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, PSYCInfo, and CINAHL, to identify relevant randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The inclusion criteria for the analysis were RCTs that compared GnRHas with no treatment, placebo, danazol, intrauterine progestogens, or other GnRHas for the treatment of endometriosis-related pain. Trials involving add-back therapy, oral contraceptives, surgical interventions, GnRH antagonists, or complementary therapies were excluded. Data extraction and quality assessment were conducted independently by two reviewers. Pain relief was designated as the primary outcome, with relative risk used for dichotomous data and mean differences or standardized mean differences applied for continuous data. A total of 41 trials, encompassing 4935 women, were included in the analysis. The evidence regarding whether GnRHas were more effective than no treatment or placebo in relieving symptoms was inconsistent and of low quality. Similarly, the evidence comparing GnRHas to danazol was inconsistent and of low or very low quality. Adverse events were reported more frequently in the GnRHa treatment groups. When comparing GnRHas to the levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS), there was no statistically significant difference in overall pain relief (standardized mean difference [SMD] -0.25, 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.60 to 0.10, P=0.46), based on moderate-quality evidence. Additionally, there was limited evidence regarding the optimal dosage, duration, and route of administration for GnRHas in this context. In conclusion, it remains unclear whether GnRHas are more effective than no treatment or placebo in alleviating pain associated with endometriosis. There was no consistent evidence to suggest a difference in pain relief between GnRHas and danazol, although adverse events were more commonly reported in the GnRHa groups. Furthermore, no significant difference in pain relief was observed between GnRHas and LNG-IUS. Notably, no studies included in the analysis compared GnRHas with analgesics.
